title: Learning Personalized Agents from Human Feedback
authors: Liang, K.; Kruk, J.; Qian, S.; Yang, X.; Bi, S.; Yao, Y.; Nie, S.; Zhang, M.; Liu, L.; Fernández Fisac, J.; Zhou, S.; Hosseini, S.
tldr: A continual personalization framework using explicit per-user memory and dual feedback channels enables agents to learn online from live interaction and adapt to non-stationary user preferences.
problem_and_motivation: Modern AI agents fail to align with individual, evolving user preferences because they rely on static datasets and cannot adapt to new users, correct mistakes from real-time feedback, or handle non-stationary preferences. Existing personalization approaches do not support learning online from live interaction, leading to a fundamental limitation in user-facing applications.
approach: Introduces PAHF, a continual personalization framework with a three-step loop: pre-action clarification, action execution, and post-action feedback integration.
Uses explicit per-user memory (SQLite or FAISS backend) updated from pre-action and post-action feedback to refine agent behavior over time.
Develops a four-phase evaluation protocol to separately test initial preference learning and adaptation to persona shifts.
Constructs two benchmarks: embodied manipulation (40 users, 1,200 scenarios per phase) and online shopping (20 users, 900 scenarios per phase).
Implements agent with GPT-4o and ReAct framework; compares No Memory, Pre-action Only, Post-action Only, and PAHF baselines.
Provides theoretical analysis proving necessity of both feedback channels for handling partial observability and non-stationarity.
Uses dense-retrieval memory with DRAGON+ embeddings and an LLM-as-judge for salience detection and memory integration.
findings: Pre-action clarification enables agents to achieve substantially higher success rates on the first interaction and lower cumulative personalization error in initial learning.
Pre-action feedback alone is brittle under preference drift; Pre-action Only agents stop asking questions and remain confidently wrong after preferences change.
Post-action feedback is essential for fast adaptation; Post-action Only agents recover to 67.9% success in embodied domain after preference drift.
num: PAHF achieves the highest success rates across all phases and domains: 70.5% in embodied Phase 4 and 70.3% in shopping Phase 4.
num: PAHF's dynamic regret bound is O(K + γT m^{-k}), with k = Θ(log_m T) yielding O(K + γ) expected mistakes.
Combining pre-action and post-action feedback with explicit memory is critical; PAHF consistently outperforms single-channel baselines.

definitions.definition: Personalized Agents from Human Feedback, a framework for continual personalization using explicit memory and dual feedback channels.
Average cumulative personalization error, a metric tracking error rate over learning iterations.
Large language model, the underlying model powering the agent's reasoning and action generation.
Retrieval-augmented generation, a technique for retrieving relevant information from memory before generating responses.
Success rate, the fraction of tasks completed correctly.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper introduces a continual personalization framework that learns online from live interaction, addressing the fundamental limitation of static personalization methods. It provides both theoretical and empirical evidence that explicit memory combined with dual feedback channels (pre-action clarification and post-action correction) is necessary for robust personalization under preference drift. The proposed four-phase evaluation protocol and two benchmarks establish a standardized way to measure an agent's ability to learn from scratch and adapt to persona shifts.
directly_justifies: Pre-action feedback is essential for preventing initial personalization errors under partial observability.
Post-action feedback is necessary for correcting miscalibrated beliefs after preference drift.
Explicit memory with dual feedback channels yields lower cumulative personalization error than single-channel baselines.
Combining both feedback channels achieves the highest success rates across all evaluation phases.
limits: The memory architecture is deliberately simple; more sophisticated memory systems could improve scalability and context retention.
The framework does not explicitly handle noisy or inconsistent human feedback, which is common in real-world settings.
Agents still struggle to achieve high success rates in the online shopping domain, indicating fine-grained preference reasoning remains challenging.
The agent is limited to at most one clarification question per task, which increases task difficulty and may not reflect real-world interaction strategies.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: A systematic scan across all topic domains flagged the following as relevant: 5.A (Financial Behavioral Profiles) because the paper directly models and updates user preference profiles; 5.B (Profile Dynamics) because it explicitly addresses cold-start and evolving preferences; 5.C (Classification Approaches) because retrieval-based memory can be viewed as a classification of preferences. For budgeting domains, 7.A (Budgeting Strategies) is relevant as the framework learns constraints, 7.B (Budget Recommendation) maps to action recommendation based on preferences, and 7.E (Onboarding) is directly addressed. Engagement topics (11.A, 11.B) were considered low relevance because the paper mentions user friction but does not study engagement or retention mechanisms. Evaluation topics (12.A, 12.C) are highly relevant due to the proposed protocol and metrics. Topics related to expense categorization, financial structure, culturally specific practices, predictive modeling, anomaly detection, mobile-first design, privacy, savings goals, synthetic data, and ML deployment were rejected as they are not covered by the paper's content. The paper's overall topical coverage centers on algorithmic personalization and evaluation, with strong overlap in behavioral profile modeling and budgeting strategy domains.
